key_terms.meaning: Many modulated optical carriers of different wavelengths share one fiber, each wavelength carrying its own independent channel.
The gap Δλ (or Δf) between neighbouring channels; 100 GHz at 1550 nm equals about 0.8 nm.
WDM with narrow spacing and many channels on one fiber, so capacity grows with channel count.
Planar device with an array of curved waveguides whose interference splits or combines wavelengths.
Two fibers twisted, melted and pulled so light couples across; specified by splitting ratio (%), excess loss (dB) and directivity.
One-way component that passes light forward and blocks backward reflections, protecting lasers and amplifiers.
Periodic index variation in the core; it reflects a narrow band at the Bragg wavelength λ_B = 2 n_eff Λ, where Λ is the grating period.
Silica fiber doped with Er³⁺ ions, pumped at 980 nm or 1480 nm, giving gain in the 1530–1565 nm band.
G = P_out / P_in; in decibels, G_dB = 10 log₁₀(P_out / P_in).
NF = 10 log₁₀(F) with F = SNR_in / SNR_out; an EDFA typically gives about 4–6 dB.
A forward-biased p-n junction waveguide with anti-reflection coated facets, giving gain near 1300 nm and 1550 nm.
n = n₀ + n₂I, where n₂ ≈ 2.6×10⁻²⁰ m²/W for silica, so the refractive index follows the pulse intensity I.
Intensity-dependent phase φ_NL = (2π/λ) n₂ I L, which chirps the pulse and broadens its spectrum.
D = d(1/v_g)/dλ in ps/(nm·km); different wavelengths travel at different speeds and the pulse spreads.
A pulse whose SPM chirp exactly cancels GVD, so its shape stays fixed over long distances.
The N = 1 case, with peak power P₀ = |β₂| / (γ T₀²), where T₀ is pulse width, β₂ the GVD and γ the nonlinear coefficient.
An end-to-end optical connection that carries one wavelength from source to destination through intermediate nodes.
Node that drops chosen wavelengths to local equipment and adds new ones, passing all other wavelengths through unchanged.
A lightpath must use the same wavelength on every link of its route unless a wavelength converter is present.
Fixed 53-byte cell (5-byte header plus 48-byte payload) that carries voice, video and data on one optical pipe.

takeaways: WDM raises fiber capacity by adding wavelengths, not by making the electronics faster, so one fiber behaves like many parallel channels.
Passive components — couplers, isolators, circulators and gratings — set the insertion loss, crosstalk and reflection performance of a WDM link.
An optical amplifier boosts light directly by stimulated emission, replacing the receiver–electronics–transmitter chain at every span.
EDFA dominates 1550 nm links with high gain, low noise figure and no polarisation dependence, while SOA is smaller, cheaper and works near 1300 nm.
At high power the Kerr effect makes the pulse chirp itself through SPM; balanced against GVD, this produces a soliton that keeps its shape.
A lightpath is one wavelength held end to end, and finding wavelengths for many lightpaths is the central design problem of a WDM network.
SONET/SDH multiplexes low-rate tributaries into a frame locked to one master clock, so a single channel can be added or dropped cleanly.
WDM nodes combine add-drop, cross-connection and sometimes wavelength conversion, and the choice of converter placement decides network blocking.
Layering keeps transmission, framing and user services independent, which is why SONET/SDH, ATM and IP can share the same fiber.
bank_note: Long answers are expected to combine a labelled block diagram with the governing formula, the typical numeric values, and a clear statement of the trade-off or design choice.

bank.q: Define WDM. Explain how it increases the capacity of one fiber without raising the electronic bit rate, and list four advantages and two problems it brings.
outline: Definition: several modulated wavelengths on one fiber, each an independent channel
Capacity = number of channels × per-channel bit rate
No need for faster electronics at each end; one fiber replaces many fibers
Advantages: capacity, upgradability, transparency to bit rate and format, fewer fibers and amplifiers
Problems: wavelength assignment, crosstalk and nonlinearity, need for wavelength-stable lasers and filters
Sketch of a multiplexer–fiber–demultiplexer link

bank.q: Describe the construction and working of a fused-fiber coupler and an arrayed waveguide grating. Give the parameters used to specify each.
outline: Fused coupler: two fibers twisted, melted and pulled; power couples through the cladding region
Ports 1–4, splitting ratio in %, excess loss in dB, directivity or isolation
AWG: input slab, array of curved waveguides with fixed path differences, output slab
Interference sends each wavelength to a different output port
Parameters: channel spacing, number of channels, insertion loss, crosstalk
Comparison: AWG better for many channels; coupler cheap and simple

bank.q: Draw the block diagram of an EDFA and explain the role of the pump laser, the doped fiber and the isolators. State typical gain, noise figure and pump wavelengths.
outline: Diagram: input isolator, WDM coupler, Er³⁺-doped fiber, pump laser, output isolator, filter
Pump at 980 nm or 1480 nm excites Er³⁺ to a metastable level
Signal photon at 1530–1565 nm triggers stimulated emission and is amplified
Isolators stop reflections and pump back-flow; filter removes leftover pump
Typical gain 20–40 dB, noise figure 4–6 dB
Energy-level sketch and statement of why 980 nm gives lower noise figure

bank.q: Explain self-phase modulation. Starting from n = n₀ + n₂I, derive the intensity-dependent phase shift and the resulting frequency chirp.
outline: Kerr effect: n = n₀ + n₂I, n₂ ≈ 2.6×10⁻²⁰ m²/W
Propagation phase φ = (2π/λ)(n₀ + n₂I)L
Nonlinear phase φ_NL = γ P L with γ = 2π n₂/(λ A_eff)
Chirp δω = −dφ_NL/dt, proportional to −dP/dt
Leading edge red-shifted, trailing edge blue-shifted
Result: spectral broadening, no change of pulse shape on its own

bank.q: Describe the SONET/SDH frame and explain how a single low-rate channel can be added or dropped without breaking the whole signal apart.
outline: STS-1 frame: 810 bytes, 90 columns × 9 rows, 125 µs, 51.84 Mbit/s
STM-1 = 155.52 Mbit/s, integer multiples for higher rates
Payload envelopes, pointers and section/line/path overheads
Synchronous multiplexing locked to one master clock, so tributaries keep fixed positions
Pointer allows add/drop of one channel without full demultiplexing
Protection switching and management overhead

bank.q: A WDM link carries 40 channels spaced 100 GHz apart around 1550 nm. Find the channel spacing in nm and the total usable bandwidth in THz.
outline: Use Δλ ≈ (λ²/c) Δf
Total bandwidth = 40 × 100 GHz = 4 THz
Span in wavelength ≈ 40 × 0.8 = 32 nm around 1550 nm
Comment: fits inside the C band, spacing set by laser stability and filter passband

bank.q: An EDFA gives 25 dB gain for an input of −20 dBm. Find the output power in dBm and mW. If the input signal-to-noise ratio is 40 dB and the output is 35 dB, find the noise figure.
outline: P_out(dBm) = P_in(dBm) + G(dB) = −20 + 25 = +5 dBm
NF = SNR_in − SNR_out = 40 − 35 = 5 dB
State that NF = 10 log₁₀ F, so F ≈ 3.16
Comment: amplifier adds spontaneous emission noise

bank.q: A soliton of width T₀ = 10 ps travels in a fiber with β₂ = −20 ps²/km and γ = 2 W⁻¹km⁻¹. Find the dispersion length, the nonlinear length at the fundamental-soliton peak power, and that peak power.
outline: L_D = T₀²/|β₂| = (10)²/20 = 5 km
Check N² = L_D/L_NL = 1, confirming the fundamental soliton
Comment: 100 mW peak is high, so soliton systems need short pulses or low γ

bank.q: A 2×2 fused coupler has a 50:50 splitting ratio and 0.2 dB excess loss. With 1 mW at port 1 and nothing at port 2, find the power at each output port in dBm and mW.
outline: 1 mW = 0 dBm at the input
Split costs 10 log₁₀(1/2) = −3.01 dB per port
Add excess loss 0.2 dB
Each output ≈ −3.2 dBm ≈ 0.48 mW
Comment on directivity and how the coupling ratio varies with wavelength

bank.q: A four-node WDM ring needs one lightpath between every pair of nodes. Assign wavelengths so that the number of wavelengths is the minimum, and justify the assignment.
outline: Six lightpaths for four nodes (full mesh)
On a ring each link carries several lightpaths; lightpaths sharing a link need different wavelengths
Colouring of the path graph; lower bound from the largest number of paths on one link
Show a valid assignment with 3 wavelengths and prove 2 is impossible
State the wavelength continuity constraint used in the argument

bank.q: Compare SOA and EDFA for a 10-channel WDM link in gain band, noise figure, polarisation dependence, crosstalk, size and cost. Recommend one for a long-haul link and justify.
outline: EDFA: 1530–1565 nm, gain 20–40 dB, NF ≈ 4–6 dB, polarisation independent, slow gain dynamics so little inter-channel crosstalk, bulky, needs pump at 980/1480 nm
SOA: 1300 and 1550 nm, gain ≈ 20 dB, NF ≈ 7–9 dB, polarisation dependent unless strained, fast gain dynamics causing cross-gain modulation between channels, small and cheap
EDFA for long haul: higher gain, lower NF, no pattern-dependent crosstalk
SOA for access, switching and 1300 nm window, and for nonlinear gate applications
Justified recommendation with the numbers quoted

bank.q: Explain how SPM and GVD interact in a fiber. Derive the condition for soliton formation and discuss the practical limits on soliton communication systems.
outline: GVD: β₂ < 0 in the anomalous region, red travels faster than blue
SPM: leading edge red-shifted, trailing edge blue-shifted; in anomalous GVD the red edge slows and the blue edge speeds up
Balanced case: nonlinear Schrödinger equation with equal dispersion and nonlinear lengths
Fundamental soliton N = 1, P₀ = |β₂|/(γ T₀²), shape sech²
Higher-order solitons breathe periodically
Limits: high peak power, amplifier noise and timing jitter, soliton interaction, need for dispersion-managed or loss-managed design

bank.q: Explain the wavelength continuity constraint and blocking in WDM networks. Compare networks with no converters, sparse converters and full conversion at every node.
outline: Lightpath = one wavelength end to end; same wavelength on every link without conversion
Rerouting and wavelength reassignment reduce blocking but may not remove it
No converters: cheapest, highest blocking, wavelength assignment is a graph-colouring problem
Sparse converters: place at selected nodes, near-optimal blocking at much lower cost
Full conversion: lowest blocking, highest cost and complexity; O-E-O or all-optical conversion
Layer comparison with circuit switching and with SONET add-drop
Recommendation based on traffic load and cost

bank.q: Explain the OSI seven-layer model, place SONET/SDH and ATM in it, and discuss why ATM used fixed 53-byte cells.
outline: Seven layers: physical, data link, network, transport, session, presentation, application
SONET/SDH mainly physical layer with some data-link functions; ATM is layer 2
ATM cell: 5-byte header, 48-byte payload; small fixed size gives short, predictable packetisation delay for voice
Fixed size simplifies hardware switching and allows uniform QoS classes
Virtual circuits, VPI/VCI labels, traffic classes
Evaluate: lost to IP and Ethernet on cost and simplicity, though its QoS ideas survive

glossary.def: The drop in optical power caused by putting a component into the link, in dB.
The part of a coupler's loss not explained by the intended splitting ratio.
Leakage of one WDM channel into a neighbouring channel, measured in dB.
The fraction of input power that leaks backwards to the input-side port of a coupler.
A multi-port passive device that passes light in one rotational direction only, e.g. port 1 to 2 to 3.
Dielectric multilayer filter that passes one wavelength band and reflects the rest, used in add-drop modules.
A laser at 980 nm or 1480 nm whose power excites the erbium ions in an EDFA.
A state where more ions or carriers sit in the upper energy level than the lower one, so stimulated emission exceeds absorption.
Random photon emission that seeds amplifier noise and limits the noise figure.
The range of wavelengths over which an amplifier gives useful gain.
The output power at which amplifier gain falls 3 dB below its small-signal value.
Gain that differs for different input polarisations, a drawback of ordinary SOAs.
One channel's power changes the SOA gain seen by other channels, causing crosstalk.
L_D = T₀²/|β₂|, the distance over which GVD broadens a pulse noticeably.
L_NL = 1/(γP₀), the distance over which SPM becomes significant.
The propagation equation combining GVD and SPM that governs pulse shape in a fiber.
A change of instantaneous frequency across a pulse, so different parts of the pulse have different wavelengths.
The regime where β₂ < 0 and longer wavelengths travel faster; required for bright solitons.
A device that shifts a lightpath from one wavelength to another, removing the continuity constraint.
A node that switches wavelengths from any input fiber to any output fiber.
The chance that a requested lightpath cannot be set up because no wavelength is free.
Packing tributary channels into fixed positions of a frame locked to one master clock.
Nearly but not exactly synchronous, so bit stuffing is needed before multiplexing, as in the PDH hierarchy.
SONET/SDH overhead bytes used for framing, error checking and management at each level.
One level of a layered model that performs a defined job and uses the services of the level below.
A connection whose route is fixed at setup time and identified by a short label in each cell.
